[
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/fisher-ftns",
    "title": "Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection (partial-change form)",
    "statement": "The rate of increase in mean fitness of a population due to natural selection equals its additive genetic variance in fitness at that time.",
    "math": "\\Delta_{NS}\\bar{w} = V_A(w)/\\bar{w} (discrete generations); \\left.\\frac{d\\bar{m}}{dt}\\right|_{NS} = V_A(m) for Malthusian fitness m",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/fisher-ftns.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/fisher-infinitesimal",
    "title": "Fisher's infinitesimal model of quantitative inheritance",
    "statement": "Continuous traits determined by many Mendelian loci of small additive effect produce the observed correlations between relatives, so biometric and Mendelian inheritance are consistent.",
    "math": "Cov(z_i, z_j) = 2\\Theta_{ij} V_A + \\Delta_{ij} V_D; in the limit of M \\to \\infty loci the offspring trait given parents is Gaussian with mean (z_1+z_2)/2 and segregation variance V_0(1-\\bar{F}), with error O(1/\\sqrt{M}) (Barton, Etheridge and Veber 2017)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/fisher-infinitesimal.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/fisher-kpp-speed",
    "title": "Fisher-KPP wave of advance of an advantageous gene",
    "statement": "An advantageous allele spreading through a continuous population advances as a travelling wave whose speed is set by the selection coefficient and the diffusion (dispersal) rate.",
    "math": "u_t = D u_{xx} + s u(1-u); travelling waves u(x-ct) exist iff c \\ge c^* = 2\\sqrt{sD}; compactly supported initial data spread at asymptotic speed c^*",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/fisher-kpp-speed.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/fisher-sex-ratio",
    "title": "Fisher's principle of equal investment in the sexes",
    "statement": "Under random mating and autosomal inheritance, selection drives parents to invest equally in sons and daughters, which gives a 1:1 sex ratio when the two cost the same.",
    "math": "ESS allocation: N_m c_m = N_f c_f; with c_m = c_f the unbeatable primary sex ratio is 1:1",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/fisher-sex-ratio.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/hamilton-haplodiploidy",
    "title": "Haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality",
    "statement": "Because full sisters in haplodiploid species share three quarters of their genes, more than a mother shares with her offspring, haplodiploid insects are predisposed to evolve sterile worker castes.",
    "math": "with a singly mated queen, r_{sister,sister} = 3/4 > r_{mother,daughter} = 1/2, but r_{sister,brother} = 1/4",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/hamilton-haplodiploidy.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/hamilton-lmc",
    "title": "Local mate competition sex ratio",
    "statement": "When a few mothers lay eggs on a patch and their offspring mate there before the daughters disperse, the evolutionarily stable sex ratio is female-biased, and the bias weakens as the number of mothers grows.",
    "math": "unbeatable proportion of males x^* = \\frac{n-1}{2n} for n foundresses per patch (diploid case)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/hamilton-lmc.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/hamilton-rule",
    "title": "Hamilton's rule",
    "statement": "A gene for social behaviour increases in frequency when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by genetic relatedness, exceeds the cost to the actor.",
    "math": "\\Delta \\bar{p} > 0 \\iff r b - c > 0, with r, b, c defined as regression coefficients (Queller form via the Price equation)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/hamilton-rule.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/hamilton-senescence",
    "title": "Declining force of selection with age",
    "statement": "The strength of selection on survival falls with age after reproduction begins, so senescence is an inevitable outcome of natural selection.",
    "math": "s(a) = \\frac{\\partial r}{\\partial \\ln p_a} = \\frac{1}{T}\\sum_{x=a+1}^{\\infty} e^{-rx} l_x m_x, non-increasing in a",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/hamilton-senescence.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/kimura-fixation-probability",
    "title": "Kimura fixation probability of a mutant allele",
    "statement": "The probability that a mutant allele eventually fixes in a finite population depends on its initial frequency, its selective advantage and the effective population size, and equals its initial frequency when it is neutral.",
    "math": "u(p) = \\frac{1-e^{-4N_e s p}}{1-e^{-4N_e s}}; neutral limit u(p) = p, so a new mutant fixes with probability 1/(2N)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/kimura-fixation-probability.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/kimura-fixation-time",
    "title": "Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutant",
    "statement": "A neutral mutant that does go to fixation takes on average about four times the effective population size, in generations, to do so.",
    "math": "\\bar{t}_1(p) = -\\frac{4N_e(1-p)\\ln(1-p)}{p}; as p = 1/(2N) \\to 0, \\bar{t}_1 \\to 4N_e generations",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/kimura-fixation-time.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/kimura-heterozygosity",
    "title": "Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)",
    "statement": "Under neutral mutation to new alleles and drift, expected heterozygosity reaches an equilibrium that rises with the product of effective population size and mutation rate.",
    "math": "H = \\frac{\\theta}{1+\\theta}, \\theta = 4N_e\\mu (infinite-alleles model)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/kimura-heterozygosity.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/kimura-neutral-theory",
    "title": "Neutral theory: most molecular substitutions are neutral",
    "statement": "Most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by random drift of selectively neutral or nearly neutral mutations, not by positive selection.",
    "math": "empirical claim: for most sites |N_e s| \\lesssim 1, so the fraction of substitutions driven by positive selection \\alpha is small; tested with d_N/d_S and McDonald-Kreitman \\alpha = 1 - \\frac{D_s P_n}{D_n P_s}",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/kimura-neutral-theory.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/kimura-substitution-rate",
    "title": "Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate",
    "statement": "For neutral mutations the long-run rate of molecular substitution equals the mutation rate per generation, independent of population size, which yields a molecular clock.",
    "math": "k = 2N\\mu \\cdot \\frac{1}{2N} = \\mu",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/kimura-substitution-rate.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/maynardsmith-ess",
    "title": "Evolutionarily stable strategy conditions",
    "statement": "A strategy is evolutionarily stable if, once common, it cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy.",
    "math": "I is an ESS iff for all J \\ne I: E(I,I) > E(J,I), or E(I,I) = E(J,I) and E(I,J) > E(J,J); every ESS is an asymptotically stable rest point of the replicator dynamics (Taylor and Jonker 1978), not conversely",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/maynardsmith-ess.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/maynardsmith-hawk-dove",
    "title": "Hawk-Dove mixed ESS",
    "statement": "When the cost of injury exceeds the value of the contested resource, the stable outcome is a mixture in which animals escalate with probability equal to the ratio of resource value to injury cost.",
    "math": "payoffs E(H,H) = (V-C)/2, E(H,D) = V, E(D,H) = 0, E(D,D) = V/2; for C > V the unique ESS plays Hawk with probability p^* = V/C",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/maynardsmith-hawk-dove.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/maynardsmith-hitchhiking",
    "title": "Genetic hitchhiking (selective sweep)",
    "statement": "When a favourable mutation sweeps to fixation, it reduces genetic variation at closely linked neutral sites, and the reduction is larger the tighter the linkage relative to the strength of selection.",
    "math": "the relative heterozygosity H_{after}/H_{before} at a neutral site at recombination fraction c is an increasing function of c/s that tends to 0 as c/s \\to 0; the affected region has a width of order s in recombination units, up to logarithmic factors in N",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/maynardsmith-hitchhiking.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/maynardsmith-twofold-cost",
    "title": "Twofold cost of sex",
    "statement": "An asexual mutant female in a sexual population with equal sex ratio produces twice as many grandchildren as a sexual female, so sex needs a compensating advantage of up to twofold to persist.",
    "math": "with equal fecundity and a 1:1 sex ratio, the odds of asexual to sexual females double each generation: \\frac{q_{t+1}}{1-q_{t+1}} = 2\\frac{q_t}{1-q_t}",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/maynardsmith-twofold-cost.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/maynardsmith-war-of-attrition",
    "title": "War of attrition ESS",
    "statement": "In contests settled by display, where the animal willing to persist longer wins and costs grow with time, the stable strategy is to choose a persistence time at random from an exponential distribution whose mean equals the resource value.",
    "math": "with cost linear in time at unit rate and resource value V, the ESS persistence time has density p(x) = \\frac{1}{V} e^{-x/V}",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/math-population-genetics-and-evolutionary-theory",
    "nanopub": "math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned/maynardsmith-war-of-attrition.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-01",
    "title": "Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth",
    "statement": "Weight varies as the cube of length (W = kL³) in an animal of unchanging form and density, so tracking whether k stays constant or varies with length shows whether the animal's general form changes as it grows; such changes are likely as long as growth continues.",
    "math": "W = kL^3; form unchanged during growth \\iff k constant",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-01.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-02",
    "title": "Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height",
    "statement": "For a tree to stand without buckling under its own weight, its diameter must increase as the 3/2 power of its height, which explains why young trees are slender and old large ones stunted, and sets a theoretical maximum tree height (about 300 ft for a Kew-flagstaff pine).",
    "math": "d \\propto h^{3/2} (no buckling under own weight); h_{max} \\approx 300\\,\\text{ft} for the Kew-flagstaff pine",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-02.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-03",
    "title": "Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals",
    "statement": "Because the strength of muscles and the crushing resistance of bones vary as their cross-section (the square of linear size) while body weight varies as the cube, there is a definite upper limit to the size of an animal living under gravity; the elephant, with disproportionately thick limb bones and reduced agility, is already near it.",
    "math": "strength \\propto L^2, W \\propto L^3 \\Rightarrow strength/W \\propto L^{-1}, so L is bounded above under gravity",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-03.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-05",
    "title": "Larger fish can sprint faster but cover similar distances and tire more slowly",
    "statement": "Since muscular work available scales as the cube of linear size while the rate of energy supply, depending on respiratory surface, scales only as the square, a larger fish should achieve a much higher burst speed than a smaller one but travel a similar distance over a year, and smaller individuals should fatigue faster and have less staying power.",
    "math": "W_{muscle} \\propto L^3; \\dot{E}_{supply} \\propto S \\propto L^2",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-05.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-06",
    "title": "Power needed for flight grows as length^3.5 while muscle power grows as length^3",
    "statement": "A bird of fixed proportions must fly at a minimum speed proportional to the square root of its linear size, so the work needed for flight varies as the 3½ power of linear size while the work its muscles can supply varies only as the cube; flight thus becomes harder as birds get larger (about 1.4 times harder per doubling of length).",
    "math": "V_{min} \\propto L^{1/2}; W_{flight} = mV^2 \\propto L^{7/2}; W_{muscle} \\propto L^3; per doubling of L: 2^{7/2} : 2^3 \\approx 1.4 : 1",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-06.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-09",
    "title": "Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size",
    "statement": "Because the impulse of a leap is proportional to muscle volume and so to body mass, the take-off velocity is independent of size, and similarly built animals should jump to the same actual height rather than the same relative height; longer levers in larger animals give them some advantage.",
    "math": "impulse \\propto M \\Rightarrow v_0 independent of L; jump height h = v_0^2/2g independent of L",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-09.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-10",
    "title": "Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking",
    "statement": "Leaving aside differences in mechanical construction, swimming (Froude's law), flight (minimum stable speed) and walking (the leg swinging as a pendulum) all give the same result: an animal's velocity tends to vary as the square root of its linear dimensions.",
    "math": "V \\propto L^{1/2} for swimming (Froude), flight (minimum speed) and walking (pendulum leg)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-10.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-12",
    "title": "Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass",
    "statement": "Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.",
    "math": "S/M \\approx \\text{const} maintained by change of form, against S/M \\propto L^{-1} for similar forms",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-12.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch02-15",
    "title": "Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass",
    "statement": "Cell division keeps the ratio between a cell's surface and its mass approximately constant and restores the balance of surface energy with the cell's other energies; cleavage of an egg increases surface without increasing volume or mass.",
    "math": "cell division keeps S/M \\approx \\text{const}; cleavage increases S at constant V and M",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch02-15.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch03-07",
    "title": "Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth",
    "statement": "Whatever the law of increase in a linear dimension, volume and therefore weight tend to vary as the cube of linear dimensions, which mainly (though not wholly) explains why the human weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve.",
    "math": "W \\propto L^3 whatever the law of growth L(t)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch03-07.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch03-17",
    "title": "Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity",
    "statement": "In plaice the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 is not constant but rises to a maximum and then slowly declines with increasing size, the maximum falling near 30 cm, about the size at which sexual maturity begins.",
    "math": "k = W/L^3 not constant in plaice; \\max_L k at L \\approx 30\\,\\text{cm}",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch03-17.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch03-21",
    "title": "Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction",
    "statement": "Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).",
    "math": "v(\\theta + n) = x^n v(\\theta) for a rise of n degrees; temperature coefficient of growth x^{10} \\approx 2\\text{--}3",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch03-21.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch03-23",
    "title": "Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve",
    "statement": "In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.",
    "math": "L(t) = \\bar{L}(t) + A(t)\\sin(2\\pi t / 1\\,\\text{yr}), A(t) \\to 0 as d\\bar{L}/dt \\to 0 (damped sine)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch03-23.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch03-30",
    "title": "Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time",
    "statement": "After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.",
    "math": "V^m T^n = \\text{const}; for regenerating tadpole tails V T^2 \\approx \\text{const}",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch03-30.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch05-10",
    "title": "Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms",
    "statement": "Of the six surfaces of revolution with constant mean curvature (plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid), spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest forms of small unicellular organisms and of cells in simple aggregates, and transitions between them are frequent during growth, reproduction and development.",
    "math": "1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \\text{const}; surfaces of revolution: plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch05-10.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch05-11",
    "title": "A cylindrical cell's end cap has twice the cylinder's radius and height about 0.27R",
    "statement": "Where a cylindrical cell of uniform wall tension is capped by part of a sphere, the sphere's radius is twice the cylinder's radius, the cap subtends a cone of 60°, and its height is about 0.27 of the cylinder radius (a little more than one-eighth of the diameter), proportions seen in the free end cells of Spirogyra.",
    "math": "R_{cap} = 2R; cap subtends a cone of 60^\\circ; cap height = R(2 - \\sqrt{3}) \\approx 0.27R",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch05-11.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch05-12",
    "title": "Viscid spider-thread coating breaks into beads at the cylinder stability limit",
    "statement": "The sticky fluid coating of a spider's spiral thread, being a liquid cylinder, becomes unstable when its length exceeds its circumference and breaks up into equal, equally spaced beads (often with smaller beads between), the spacing being somewhat greater than theory owing to viscosity and drag on the core thread.",
    "math": "liquid cylinder of radius r unstable for length l > 2\\pi r; breaks into equal, equally spaced beads",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
    "nanopub": "thompson-growth-form/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch05-12.trig"
  },
  {
    "claim": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/claim/thompson1917-ch05-17",
    "title": "Vorticella bells form a graded series of unduloids",
    "statement": "The bells of the various species of Vorticella, like many other Infusoria, are unduloids or partial unduloids spanning every gradation from nearly cylindrical to nearly spherical, bounded by the stalk attachment and the ciliary ring as by two unequal supporting rings, and the species differ only in ratio or degree.",
    "math": "1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \\text{const} (unduloid between two unequal supporting rings)",
    "domain": "https://w3id.org/delphi/resource/domain/thompson-growth-form-1917",
